papers.title: DarkMatterFM-Registry: A Machine-Readable Registry of Dark-Matter Models Extracted from the arXiv Literature
papers.abstract: To use a dark-matter model one needs to know what defines it, which observables it affects, which codes and likelihoods evaluate it, and under what assumptions a published bound applies. That information is scattered across tens of thousands of papers. We present DarkMatterFM-Registry, a machine-readable registry of dark-matter models extracted from arXiv full texts by a staged large-language-model (LLM) pipeline: 6,145 structured model cards, validated against a seven-file JSON Schema suite, ranked by expected value for observational follow-up, and enriched for the top ~2,000 with observables, constraints, and theory-to-observable routes. Schema checks pass 97.8% of cards, and an LLM-judged accuracy study on a stratified card sample finds 81% of section verdicts correct, 18% partially correct, and none hallucinated. As a first application we turn the registry into a priority-weighted roadmap of 25 concrete projects the community could build. The roadmap is built by judging every computational step of every enriched model's theory-to-observable routes as available, partial, or missing, and aggregating the resulting typed gaps weighted by model priority. We find that what blocks the most high-priority models is not missing theory but missing shared infrastructure: model files for existing relic-abundance solvers, a general non-cold Boltzmann-code framework, reusable indirect-detection likelihoods, and a Lyman-$\alpha$ forest likelihood for non-cold dark matter (the largest gap for structure-formation probes). The model cards, schemas, roadmap, and ranking are released making the project reproducible and the cards available for the community.

papers.title: Interferometric survey of stellar parameters. Reliable methodology for a direct measurement of the angular diameter in exoplanet host stars
authors: R. V. Iba\~nez Bustos (Universit\'e C\^ote d'Azur
G. Schaefer (The CHARA Array of Georgia State University
A. Domiciano de Souza (Universit\'e C\^ote d'Azur
N. Anugu (The CHARA Array of Georgia State University
papers.abstract: Since their pioneer observations more than thirty years ago, exoplanets have been a major topic among the astrophysics community. Despite their ubiquity, our knowledge of planetary parameters and internal compositions still mostly relies on stellar quantities estimated through evolutionary models, which suffer from a calibration bias, preventing the community to have accurate discussions on the diversity of planets across the Universe. We use our sample to demonstrate the current best reachable precision of the CHARA Array to be $\sim$ 2% on radius determination, with an error budget dominated by the uncertainty on the angular diameter, while systematics are shown to be of the order of 1% thanks to our methodology. While the precision matches values found in the literature, we demonstrate the uniqueness of the present study in the relevance of the results put forward. Finally, we show that our methods naturally translate into an improved accuracy of the planetary parameters, along with an improvement in precision by $\sim$ 50% in radius and $\sim$ 30% in mass.

papers.title: System noise temperature measurements of a 19-element phased array feed
papers.abstract: We present multi-epoch system noise temperature measurements of a 19 element hexagonal room-temperature phased array feed (PAF) using a modified Y-factor method. A Python-based pipeline with iterative channel calibration and maxSNR beam forming is developed to do data reduction, and a covariance-based decomposition scheme is proposed to extract mutual coupling noise temperature Tmc. Long-term observations from March to June 2026 capture temporal receiver noise drift mainly induced by LNA temperature variations. Within the 1.37-1.47 GHz operating band, the measured beam equivalent system noise temperature of the PAF is about 73-89 K. The measured Tmc baseline ranges from about 2 K to 8 K, while under thermal loading, the resonant peak of Tmc can increase to more than 20 K. The baseline of Tmc is consistent with the S-parameter mea surements, which show the Tmc of the full array ranges less than 10.7 K. The baseline fluctuation of Tmc most likely arises from the superposition of thermal and non-thermal components of the spatial electromagnetic fields. A detachable stainless steel shield is deployed to quantify sidelobe spillover noise, and comparative tests show unshielded en vironmental interference increases receiver noise temperature by over 60 K. The proposed measurements and data processing framework provides a practical reference for noise per formance characterization of ground-based radio telescope PAF prototypes.

papers.title: Estimations for strong and weak hot Jupiter magnetism: A Python package with interpolators and scaling laws
papers.abstract: Hot Jupiters (HJs) are commonly thought to host the strongest dynamo-generated magnetic fields among exoplanets, exceeding Jupiter's by up to an order of magnitude, which can potentially induce observable star-planet interaction (SPI) and planetary radio emission. However, while several indirect, model-dependent estimates of HJ magnetic fields have been reported from SPIs and recent transmission spectroscopy diagnostics, no unambiguous direct (radio) detection has yet been achieved. We aim to provide a range of magnetic field estimates for HJs, considering the mechanisms responsible for inflation and the convective flux entering the magnetic field scaling law. Given that their dynamos operate in the fast-rotating regime (Rossby number <~ 0.1), we combine one-dimensional evolutionary interior models with magnetic field scaling laws under two limiting heating scenarios: deep and shallow energy depositions. The deep-heating scenario maximizes convective heat flux in the dynamo and predicts strong magnetic fields of up to ~100 G, whereas shallow heating, which is arguably more realistic for most proposed physical mechanisms, weakens convection and yields much weaker fields of O(1) G. The strong field scenario is compatible with SPI indirect detections, and the weak field scenario is in agreement with recent atmospheric constraints. We derive scaling law relations based on observables (planetary mass, radius, and/or incident stellar flux): Bstrong = 19 M_P^0.6 R_P^1.7 G; Bweak = 0.8 M_P^1.5 R_P^-1.2 G. These predictions provide a framework for interpreting future atmospheric wind measurements, SPI signatures, and radio observations, which may ultimately discriminate between competing interior-heating scenarios.

papers.title: New optimisations for exact, scalable 2D Gaussian process inference, with applications to astronomical time-series
papers.abstract: Astronomical datasets often consist of a grid of datapoints in two or more dimensions, such as images, spectroscopic time-series, and imaging time-series. Gaussian processes (GPs) are a powerful tool for dealing with correlated noise in these data, arising from both astrophysical and instrumental systematics. Despite this, popular GP optimisations such as celerite are largely restricted to 1D datasets. Extensions to 2D data typically come with limited flexibility or poor scaling. As a motivating example, this limitation is significant for transiting exoplanet spectroscopy with JWST, as current analyses typically assume each spectroscopic light curve is statistically independent, despite many potential sources of wavelength-correlation, including detector readout noise and stellar granulation. This introduces a potential bias in atmospheric retrievals which is typically ignored. To solve this problem, we present new, exact GP optimisations implemented in the JAX-based package luas, which extend 1D GP optimisations to multidimensional data using Kronecker product algebra. These GP optimisations are highly flexible, permit efficient analysis of 2D datasets containing millions of datapoints, and in many cases have a cheaper cost than transit light curve modelling. These optimisations are key to pushing the limits of exoplanet spectroscopy to smaller targets around bright host stars, as we increasingly hit instrumental and astrophysical noise floors. We suggest further applications to the analysis of ground-based high resolution spectroscopic time-series, extreme precision radial velocities, and high-contrast imaging, drawing on the connection that certain 2D GP models represent a probabilistic generalisation of PCA. Applications may even extend to machine learning and geostatistics, as we present novel optimisations for the Linear Mixing Model and the Linear Model of Coregionalisation.

papers.title: Suppression of water-ice UV photodesorption on cosmic dust analogs
papers.abstract: Ultraviolet (UV) photodesorption regulates the partitioning of water between interstellar ice mantles and the gas phase, yet laboratory yields are generally measured on planar substrates rather than on surfaces representative of cosmic dust. We investigate how grain morphology affects UV photodesorption from thin H$_2$O ice films of 2-6 monolayers deposited on planar gold and olivine, soot nanoparticles, and olivine microparticles. Samples were irradiated at 12 and 60 K with a microwave-discharge hydrogen lamp, and ice depletion was monitored by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and reflection-absorption infrared spectroscopy. On planar gold, the photodesorption yield increases approximately linearly with ice coverage, from $\sim5\times10^{-4}$ to $\sim2\times10^{-3}$ molecule photon$^{-1}$ between 2 and 6 monolayers, consistent with increasing UV absorption in optically thin ice; planar olivine gives comparable yields. In contrast, photodesorption is suppressed on particulate olivine and, more strongly, on soot, where yields are up to a factor of $\sim40$ lower than on gold at 12 K. Both experimental techniques confirm the strong suppression of ice depletion on soot. These results show that UV photodesorption depends not only on ice coverage but also strongly on grain morphology. The pronounced suppression on soot may reflect heterogeneous ice growth and altered energy redistribution within nanoscale ice domains, implying that yields measured on planar substrates may substantially overestimate photodesorption from the thin ice mantles of cosmic dust.

papers.title: Advances in High-Precision Astrometry for Exoplanet Detection for Astrometric Missions
papers.abstract: High-precision astrometry is a cornerstone for detecting Earth-like exoplanets in the habitable zones of nearby solar-type stars and probing the nature of dark matter in galactic environments. Achieving sub-microarcsecond accuracy requires unprecedented control over detector morphology, optical distortion, and astrometric measurement techniques. This paper reviews recent progress in characterizing large format detector at the micropixel scale level, calibrating optical distortion using reference stars, and refining differential astrometry methods to detect the faint astrometric signatures of Earth-mass exoplanets. We highlight the latest developments in the RETINA project, which aims to advance the TRL of GIGAPYX 220 MP CMOS detectors from Pyxalis which are critical components for future space missions such as ESA's Theia and NASA's Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). The project focuses on precise calibration methods, including Young's fringe projection, to monitor pixel geometry and intra-pixel response across gigapixel-scale focal planes. By integrating these advancements, RETINA seeks to enable astrometric detection of Earth-mass exoplanets with a precision of few tens of micropixels on the focal plane. We discuss the technical strategies, laboratory validations, and system-level integration required to achieve these goals, emphasizing the synergy between detector technology, optical calibration, and mission design. These innovations pave the way for next-generation astrometric instruments capable of transforming our understanding of exoplanetary systems and dark matter dynamics.

papers.title: Predicting next-week VIIRS fire detections in Bolivia: a reproducible benchmark with temporal and geographic evaluation
papers.abstract: Weekly detection forecasts could help prioritize fire monitoring across Bolivia. We estimate the probability of at least one fire detection by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) on the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite in each 0.05-degree cell during the following 7 days. Primary models were fixed before test scoring. Calibrated LightGBM, a gradient-boosted decision-tree model, reaches 2023-2025 temporal-test average precision (AP) of 0.323 (95% block-bootstrap interval 0.222-0.383), compared with 0.167 for climatology and 0.143 for persistence. Its paired AP gain over climatology is 0.1567 (0.0998-0.2179). A separately selected geographic model reaches AP 0.384 versus 0.181 for persistence in regions excluded from fitting. In the temporal-test population, reviewing the highest-ranked 5% and 10% of eligible area would have covered 38.4% and 55.8% of cell-weeks with detections. Probabilities still overestimate detection frequency in the highest-probability group. Retrospective rainfall provides no clear AP improvement; the primary validation comparisons for vegetation, land cover and their combination are inconclusive. Positive secondary or exploratory intervals do not change those decisions. Evaluation requires complete target and recent-history observations and measures satellite detections, not individual fires, causes or burned area. Prospective evaluation should archive inputs at each weekly issue and measure ranking, calibration and the usefulness of selected cells for monitoring decisions.

papers.title: Phentax: A JAX implementation of the IMRPhenomTHM waveform model
papers.abstract: The upcoming Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is expected to be sensitive to thousands of white dwarf (WD) binaries in our galaxy, extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs) of stellar-mass compact objects into massive black holes, stellar-mass black hole binaries (SOBHBs) in their early inspiral phase, and, crucially, massive black hole binaries (MBHBs) with masses in the range of $10^4$-$10^7 M_\odot$. The presence of such a large number of signals requires joint inference of all parameters across all sources present in the data, an approach referred to as "global fit". This requires evaluating hundreds of thousands of waveform templates, which can be computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we present $\texttt{Phentax}$, a $\texttt{JAX}$ re-implementation of the $\texttt{IMRPhenomTHM}$ waveform model. This is a state-of-the-art time-domain phenomenological waveform model for comparable-mass binary black holes that includes the effects of higher-order modes. Given this, $\texttt{IMRPhenomTHM}$ is one of the models currently used to simulate and analyze MBHB signals in LISA. With $\texttt{Phentax}$, we provide a fast, easy-to-batch, and differentiable implementation of this waveform model to accelerate the development of LISA global fit algorithms.

papers.title: A pipeline for identifying astrophysical signals and instrumental glitches in LISA data
papers.abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is a space-based gravitational wave detector scheduled for launch in the 2030s by the European Space Agency. Operating in the 0.1 mHz to 0.1 Hz band, LISA will observe a variety of astrophysical sources including but not limited to supermassive black hole mergers, extreme mass ratio inspirals, and white dwarf binaries. LISA will yield new insights, including supermassive black hole formation, new tests of general relativity, population studies of white dwarfs and others. Like all interferometric gravitational wave detectors, LISA data is expected to contain non-astrophysical transients, commonly referred to as glitches. We introduce a two step pipeline that consists of a search algorithm for detecting potential transients in simulated LISA data followed by a machine learning model that classifies the detected transients as gravitational waves or instrumental glitches. This is important for MBHBs with very high masses (around $10^6\ M_{\odot}$) which are transients that could be morphologically similar to LISA glitches in the data. Initial results demonstrate a promising ability to classify detected events with an accuracy close to $98\%$. The pipeline also shows the ability to analyze a month of data in under 2 minutes on a laptop. This shows an eventual utility of our pipeline for enabling accurate rapid alerts from low latency searches. It could also support model selection in global-fit analyses by providing an initial summary of the location and type of individual signals. This paper also discusses challenges encountered during training, including limitations of the current framework.

papers.title: Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit
papers.abstract: More than 13,000 satellites operate in low Earth orbit (LEO), and concern has grown that nuclear weapons could be used in space to target them. Beyond the initial X-ray burst, electrons released by radioactive fission products can become trapped in Earth's magnetic field, repeatedly exposing satellites as an artificial radiation belt. Here we couple prompt radiation, electron trapping and belt evolution to satellite failures, collisions and atmospheric drag. For a 1-Mt detonation at 500km over the South Atlantic, repeated belt exposure disables approximately 98% of modeled satellites within one week in our central case. Tripling the assumed radiation tolerance delays widespread failure by only days: approximately 97% are still disabled within two weeks. The loss of maneuverability sharply increases collision risk, with approximately 20 collisions expected within two years. Drag removes many disabled spacecraft from lower altitudes, but replacement satellites could remain exposed to radiation and debris for years. These findings show how a single detonation could devastate orbital infrastructure and support efforts to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.

papers.title: Optimal Strategies for Gravitational-Wave Memory Detection with Noise Marginalization in Pulsar Timing Arrays
papers.abstract: Current pulsar timing arrays could detect gravitational wave memory, which would provide a unique test of general relativity. In order to optimize our searches for gravitational wave memory in pulsar timing arrays, we integrate the optimal frequentist statistics for GW memory into the \texttt{enterprise} code suite. We additionally test a noise marginalized version of this statistic, and compare it's effectiveness to the simpler maximum posterior method. We perform these tests on simulated pulsar timing array with red and white noise content, as well as the NANOGrav $15$-year data set. We find no significant variations in our detection statistics between the noise-marginalized and the maximum-posterior methods for the simulated datasets, and only small variations in the NANOGrav $15$-year comparisons. We conclude that for realistic PTAs the noise-marginalization method could be useful for assigning a false alarm probability to Bayesian results, though the maximum posterior method is sufficient for identifying potentially detectable signals.

papers.title: Rapid and robust simulation-based inference for kilonovae
papers.abstract: With the next generation of both electromagnetic and gravitational wave observatories beginning to come online, rapid analysis methods for kilonova data are becoming increasingly important in astronomy. Traditional Bayesian parameter estimation using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is time-consuming and relies on explicit likelihood approximations that can break down when modeling uncertainties are significant. We develop a simulation-based inference (SBI) framework for kilonova parameter estimation using density-estimation likelihood-free inference. The framework uses a Gaussian process emulator trained on $\sim 1300$ POSSIS simulations. We demonstrate that SBI provides a rapid alternative to MCMC that is robust to likelihood misspecification. The standard Gaussian likelihood approximation fails to capture the non-Gaussian, correlated structure of emulator uncertainty; SBI learns this structure directly from forward simulations. Simulation studies show that the SBI method accurately recovers injected parameters, while the MCMC suffers from systematic bias caused by likelihood misspecification. This problem persists when analyzing AT2017gfo, where a subset of the MCMC posteriors pile up at prior boundaries and the SBI posteriors do not. The SBI framework infers a total ejecta mass of $\sim 0.087 M_{\odot}$ dominated by lanthanide-poor ejecta and excludes toroidal and peanut ejecta geometries at the 99th percentile for both components. The SBI framework generates $\sim 2 \times 10^{4}$ posterior samples in seconds.

papers.title: WindsoCC: reconstructing the wind-driven halo in MagAO-X images using wavefront sensor telemetry
papers.abstract: The wind-driven halo (WDH) is a persistent, low spatial frequency noise artifact that arises due to the servo-lag error inherent to all adaptive optics (AO) instruments. Spatial filtering may be employed to overcome this artifact, however, filtering out the WDH while simultaneously preserving signal from an extended astrophysical object of interest is exceptionally challenging. Additionally, since the WDH changes in intensity and position angle through an observation, data-driven algorithms (e.g., KLIP) that are commonly used to subtract the starlight need to be overly-aggressive to remove both the static and dynamic noise components. Since wavefront sensors (WFSs) continuously track the closed-loop residual wavefront error, WFS telemetry presents the ideal resource for combating this type of noise artifact through postprocessing. Using archival WFS telemetry from MagAO-X, which is the ``extreme" AO instrument for the 6.5-meter Magellan-Clay telescope, we demonstrate a novel workflow for WDH reconstruction and removal in individual coronagraphic science images. MagAO-X is equipped with a pyramid WFS capable of recording wavefront telemetry at a high-cadence which is saved during data acquisition. Given this, we detail how our WFS data processing pipeline, windsoCC, cross-correlates the recorded closed-loop wavefront to measure the wind vectors of several turbulent layers of the atmosphere above Las Campanas Observatory. We then make use of the wind parameters learned through windsoCC to reconstruct the WDH footprint by leveraging a parametric model. Notably, we demonstrate a dramatic improvement in object recovery using on-sky MagAO-X images of the disk around HR~4796A at visible wavelengths.

papers.title: Towards Genuine Coexistence: Per-Satellite Emission and Radiation Limits to Protect Radio Astronomy and Geodetic VLBI at 1-14 GHz from Satellite Constellations
papers.abstract: Geodetic very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) is a vulnerable application of the radio astronomy service (RAS): it provides the fundamental link between the celestial and terrestrial reference frames, and is the only technique that uniquely determines UT1-UTC. The next-generation geodetic VLBI Global Observing System (VGOS) achieves millimetre accuracy by synthesising group delay across 3-14 GHz using 32x32 MHz channels, most of which lie outside RAS primary allocations. The SNIFFLES-I survey (Indermuehle et al 2026) measured intended emissions, unwanted emissions (spurious emissions, notably harmonics), and unintended electromagnetic radiation (UEMR) of NGSO systems from 1-26 GHz. On this basis we model the equivalent power flux density (EPFD) of current and future constellations and compare against protection criteria of ITU-R RA.769. The analysis extends to frequencies without radio astronomy allocations where SNIFFLES-I made detections. For geodetic VLBI, we run a Monte-Carlo EPFD model at the AuScope VGOS stations and scale the aggregate from the present catalogued fleet (~12000 satellites) to the hundreds of thousands on file with a validated method. Inverting the EPFD analysis against the interpolated RA.769 thresholds yields maximum tolerable per-satellite levels for spurious emissions and for UEMR, expressed as a field-strength limit in dB(uV/m) at 10 m for standard-setting bodies. We treat proposed orbital-data-centres in Sun-synchronous orbit as a distinctively UEMR-dominated case. We find that already today the single-dish protection criteria are exceeded in two primary RAS bands. For geodetic VLBI, the dominant threat is spurious emission from the 2620 MHz Direct-to-device (DTD) downlink, whose second harmonic at 5240 MHz already causes at least 59% data loss today. (Abstract modified for arxiv limits)

papers.title: Amortized Opacity Marginalization Improves C/O Interval Calibration for Brown-Dwarf Retrievals
papers.abstract: Molecular line lists disagree at a level that measurably shifts retrieved C/O, so retrievals conditioned on a single list omit a dominant systematic from their error bars. Classical marginalization re-runs a full retrieval under K opacity realizations per object. We move that cost into simulation: while generating the training set we randomize opacities (smooth multiplicative Fourier fields in log(nu) plus a discrete line-list mixture, under a deliberately broad prior informed by measured inter-list differences), so a neural posterior estimator learns an already-marginalized posterior. On perturbed held-out spectra (n=2048) a standard NPE covers nominal 90% C/O intervals 43.3% of the time against 82.4% for a compute-matched marginalized network; three-seed control ensembles reach 93.2% on clean data but 61.4% under perturbation, against 89.4% marginalized, isolating the deficit as opacity-induced (TARP joint expected-coverage deviation 0.005 against 0.035 for a single control network). An axis ablation traces the gain to the continuous field (45.4% for the discrete swaps alone, 79.3% for the field alone). In simulation, real JWST bad-pixel masks with median filling cut the marginalized ensemble's C/O coverage from 0.894 to 0.683; an ensemble retrained with mask augmentation holds 0.918 under the full deployment preprocessing (n=1024). We apply the networks to one pipeline-combined JWST/NIRSpec G395H spectrum each of 14 late-T and Y dwarfs. The recommended mask-augmented ensemble returns C/O medians between 0.24 and 0.62 and contains the Hood et al. (2024) value of 0.53 for the T8 benchmark 2MASS J0415-0935, which every fixed-opacity control network excludes. With 90% intervals spanning about 0.43 of the prior width, this is a consistency check, not a validation.

papers.title: The Science Potential of Characterizing Gas Giant Exoplanets with HWO
authors: Beck Dacus (University of California San Diego)
Jean-Baptiste Ruffio (University of California San Diego)
Quinn Konopacky (University of California San Diego)
Mary Anne Limbach (University of Michigan Ann Arbor)
Bruce Macintosh (University of California Santa Cruz
Bertrand Mennesson (NASA Goddard Space Flight Center)
Marshall D. Perrin (Space Telescope Science Institute)
Corey Spohn (NASA Goddard Space Flight Center)
Connor Vancil (University of California Santa Barbara)
Nicole Wolff (University of California Santa Cruz)
Shelley Wright (University of California San Diego)
papers.abstract: With the ability to directly image Earth-like exoplanets and search their atmospheres for biosignatures, the upcoming Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will also collect high signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) reflected-light photometry and spectra of nearby gas giant exoplanets. Such high-quality data would allow investigations into the formation and evolution of low-mass, low-temperature gas giants, and could enable the detection of exomoons around these planets. We use the EXOSIMS direct imaging mission simulator to model HWO observations of Jupiter-radius gas giants at Earth-like and Jupiter-like instellations around the 164 stars in the ExEP target list. We find that HWO should be able to achieve S/N $\geq$ 5 broadband visible-light detections of gas giants in this instellation range within 5 minutes of integration. 10 hours of R=1000 near-IR spectroscopy with HWO should reveal water, methane, and ammonia absorption features in the atmospheres of Jupiter-like gas giants. HWO time-series photometry should exceed 1% flux precision in one hour for any Earth-instellation gas giants around ExEP stars, and for Jupiter-like gas giants at $d\leq$ 7 parsecs. Time-series light curves at this cadence and precision could, over tens of hours, reveal rotation-induced variability comparable to Jupiter's. Eclipses of Mars-sized exomoons may be detectable in high-cadence light curves of Jupiter sized planets in the habitable zones of ExEP stars at $d\leq$ 10 parsecs. For any hypothetical Earth-like exomoons with oxygen-rich atmospheres at $d\leq$ 7 parsecs from the Solar System, HWO might be able to detect the spectral signature of molecular oxygen amid the parent planet's photon noise in deep ($\sim$400 hour integration) spectroscopic HWO observations at R=1000. Such moons, if they exist, represent additional habitable worlds that HWO could investigate for biosignatures.

papers.title: Grid Optimization for Wide Field Modulation Collimators
papers.abstract: Wide-field localization of transient sources such as gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) places new demands on the grid design of modulation collimators, whose usable field of view (FOV) is normally limited by self-vignetting. A grid slat thick enough to be opaque at the energies of interest also clips off-axis rays, shrinking the effective slit width and ultimately defining the FOV itself. Historical bigrid or rotating-modulation-collimator (RMC) designs have been designed with this trade-off as an unavoidable consequence of geometric optics. We explore whether the cross-sectional shape of the grid slats can be optimized for wide FOV applications. We derive a general transmission-function framework for a bigrid pair in terms of an effective slit width that depends on slat geometry and use it to compare four slat cross sections: the conventional rectangular slat, an idealized diamond profile, a hexagonal profile that approximates photochemical etching, and the circular wire grids of early X-ray astronomy. We show that for the same bigrid pitch and thickness, a diamond profile extends the FOV and eliminates clipping throughout most of the field. We also demonstrate that a hexagonal profile achievable with standard tungsten etching factors captures many of the benefits of the idealized diamond profile. Extending the analysis to the four-phase demodulation, we show that slat shape directly sets the extent of the resulting phase-space blind spots, and that the diamond profile removes them entirely across a target FOV where the rectangular baseline cannot. We further show that finite grid opacity is a largely separable effect. Leakage through the grid leaves the geometric blind-spot boundaries unchanged. These results identify slat cross-sectional shape as a design parameter that can substantially increase throughput and widen the blind-spot-free field of view of a wide-field modulation collimator.
